query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
generation.mechanism: Plastic deformation through movement of dislocations
generation.falsification_experiment: Cooperative deformation in high-entropy alloys at ultralow temperatures

cited_evidence.text:
Paper node: Controlling Factors for the Brittle-to-Ductile Transition in Tungsten Single Crystals (1998). Cited 343 times before the cutoff; 1 papers in this graph say something specific about it.
What citing papers say about it:
- finding (from "Cooperative deformation in high-entropy alloys at ultralow temperatures", 2020): a ductile-to-brittle transition is expected because the atomic mobility vanishes, limiting plastic deformation through movement of dislocations [system Tungsten Single Crystals]
